questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: She prefers tea ____ coffee.
questions.explanation: 'Prefer X to Y' — ALWAYS 'to', NEVER 'than'. Same with 'superior/inferior/junior/senior/prior to'. This is the most frequently tested preposition trap.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: He was accused ____ theft.
questions.explanation: 'Accused OF' (the offence) vs 'charged WITH' (the offence). Both mean similar things, but the preposition is fixed and examiners swap them to test.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: She died ____ malaria last year.
questions.explanation: 'Die OF' a disease; 'die FROM' an injury or exhaustion; 'die BY' a weapon/hand of; 'die FOR' a cause. Malaria is a disease → 'of'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: The committee consists ____ seven members.
questions.explanation: 'Consist OF' (parts that make up a whole). Also: 'comprise' takes NO preposition ('The committee comprises seven members'). 'Comprise of' is often tested as wrong.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: My views differ ____ yours.
questions.explanation: Differ FROM (things / opinions that are different) vs differ WITH (a PERSON you disagree with). 'My views differ from yours' = different views; 'I differ with him' = I disagree.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: She is good ____ painting.
questions.explanation: 'Good AT / bad AT / clever AT / expert AT' a skill. 'Good in' is a common error. Similarly 'interested IN', 'experienced IN'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: Please don't look ____ on those less fortunate than you.
questions.explanation: Phrasal 'look down on' = despise. 'Look up to' = admire. 'Look into' = investigate. 'Look over' = inspect. Each is fixed.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: Ravi is married ____ Anita.
questions.explanation: 'Married TO' a person. 'Married with' is wrong (common error translated from some Indian languages). Also 'engaged to'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: The meeting was scheduled ____ 10 a.m. ____ Monday.
questions.explanation: Time rules: AT clock time, ON day/date, IN month/year/longer period. '10 a.m.' is clock time (at), 'Monday' is a day (on).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: We must refrain ____ making personal attacks.
questions.explanation: 'Refrain FROM', 'abstain FROM', 'prevent FROM', 'suffer FROM', 'prohibit FROM'. The 'from' family of verbs is a common error zone.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses the correct preposition with the verb 'congratulate'?

options.option_text: The principal congratulated the topper for securing the first rank.
The principal congratulated the topper on securing the first rank.
The principal congratulated the topper about securing the first rank.
The principal congratulated the topper at securing the first rank.

questions.explanation: 'Congratulate' is always followed by 'on' when referring to an achievement — 'congratulate someone on something' is the fixed collocation. Option A ('for') is the most tempting distractor because 'for' can denote reason, but 'congratulate for' is non-standard in formal English. Options C and D are clearly unidiomatic.

questions.stem: Identify the grammatically correct sentence using 'deprived' with the appropriate preposition.

options.option_text: Millions of rural children were deprived about quality education.
Millions of rural children were deprived from quality education.
Millions of rural children were deprived against quality education.
Millions of rural children were deprived of quality education.

questions.explanation: 'Deprived of' is the fixed collocation meaning to have something withheld or taken away. Option B ('deprived from') is the most common error, modelled by analogy on 'derived from', but the standard pair is always 'deprived of'. Options A and C are clearly non-standard.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Prolonged drought can result ____ severe food shortages and widespread economic decline.'

options.option_text: from — indicating a starting cause or origin
in — indicating an outcome or consequence
to — marking a direction or destination

questions.explanation: 'Result in' means to cause or lead to a particular outcome. Option A ('result from') is the key distractor — it shows cause, not effect (e.g., 'food shortage results from drought'), so the direction is reversed here. 'Result into' is non-standard in formal English, and 'result to' is not a recognized collocation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The young researcher was so absorbed ____ her thesis that she skipped two meals.'

options.option_text: in — correct: absorbed in means deeply focused on
into — implying physical entry or transformation
by — used to introduce the agent in passive voice
with — suggesting accompaniment or used with tools

questions.explanation: 'Absorbed in' is the fixed phrase for being deeply engrossed in an activity or thought. Option C ('absorbed by') is the key distractor — it is used in passive constructions to show the agent (e.g., 'heat was absorbed by the surface'), not for mental concentration. 'Absorbed into' implies organizational or physical merging, while 'absorbed with' is simply non-standard.

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct sentence using 'object' with the right preposition.

options.option_text: The residents strongly objected against the proposed highway construction.
The residents strongly objected about the proposed highway construction.
The residents strongly objected to the proposed highway construction.
The residents strongly objected for the proposed highway construction.

questions.explanation: The verb 'object' takes the preposition 'to' as its fixed pair — 'object to something'. Option A ('objected against') is the most common error, influenced by the conceptual sense of opposition, but 'against' is not used with 'object' in standard grammar. Options B and D are also non-standard collocations.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The latest census data appears to be at variance ____ the projections made by the national planning body.'

options.option_text: from — used for separation or point of difference
against — used to imply direct opposition or conflict
to — typically used for direction or comparison
with — correct fixed idiom: 'at variance with'

questions.explanation: The fixed idiom 'at variance with' means in disagreement or inconsistency with something, and 'with' is mandatory. Option A ('at variance from') is the most tempting error — candidates familiar with 'differ from' incorrectly substitute 'from', but the idiom is locked to 'with'. Option B ('at variance against') is not a recognized phrase in standard English.

questions.stem: Which option correctly fills both blanks? 'Every listed company must comply ____ the disclosure norms prescribed ____ SEBI.'

options.option_text: 'with' in the first blank and 'from' in the second blank
'to' in the first blank and 'by' in the second blank
'with' in the first blank and 'by' in the second blank
'to' in the first blank and 'from' in the second blank

questions.explanation: Two fixed pairs are tested simultaneously. 'Comply with' is the standard collocation (meaning to act in accordance with rules); 'comply to' is a very frequent error in formal writing. For the second blank, 'prescribed by SEBI' uses 'by' to mark the agent who prescribes — 'prescribed from' is grammatically incorrect. Option B fails on the first blank; Option A fails on the second; Option D fails on both.
